data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The fetch budget must be denominated in both requests and bytes, and exhaustion must be recorded as a typed terminal event that transitions the agent to a non-fetching state, ensuring auditability and preventing silent degradation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent can perform useful work without fetching (e.g., using cached data or local computation), then a hard terminal on budget exhaustion may be too strict and cause unnecessary termination, suggesting a soft degradation with a warning might be preferable.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If byte counting is non-deterministic due to compression or network variability, then replayability may be compromised, requiring logging of exact bytes received rather than relying on budget counters alone.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent can modify its own code to bypass the guard, then the typed terminal may not be enforced, necessitating hardware-level or OS-level resource limits.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the budget policy is complex (e.g., time-of-day limits, per-domain quotas), a simple two-counter guard may be insufficient, requiring a more expressive policy language.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The agent maintains two atomic counters: request_count and byte_count. Before each fetch, a guard checks if the next fetch would exceed either budget limit. If so, it writes a terminal event to the log containing the budget limits, current counters, and the trigger (request or byte). The agent then enters a terminal state where all fetch operations are disabled. During replay, the log's recorded fetch responses and terminal event are used to deterministically reproduce the run without re-fetching.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
